records.alt: Two discrete Poisson distributions share a rate per cell axis. One cell has widely spaced possible estimates at zero, twenty, forty hertz and so on, with probability 0.368 at zero. The twenty cell estimate has possible values one hertz apart and clusters around twenty hertz. Their means match, but the rate standard deviation falls from twenty to 4.47 hertz.
records.caption: Figure 1.1: Analytic teaching construction for the chapter’s 20 Hz, 50 ms example. The count is Poisson with mean 1 for one cell and mean 20 for 20 conditionally independent cells. Both panels plot the rate per cell 𝐾/(𝑁⁢Δ⁢𝑡), so both estimates have mean 20 Hz; their standard deviations are 20 Hz and 4.47 Hz. Each stem is a probability at one possible estimate, rather than a continuous density. Only estimates through 100 Hz are drawn. The independence condition concerns fixed modeled rates, not complete recurrent spike trains.

records.alt: Seven Brownian sample paths move irregularly above and below zero. A dashed positive and negative root mean squared envelope grows with the square root of time; some paths cross it. A second plot compares the positive root mean squared displacement with a linearly growing bias displacement. Both equal 0.40 degrees at four seconds, after which the bias line is higher.
records.caption: Figure 1.3: Simulated Brownian teaching paths and analytic displacement scales for 𝐷 =0.02 degrees squared per second and 𝑣 =0.10 degrees per second. The upper paths have zero drift and start at zero; the dashed envelope is the exact root mean squared displacement, not a boundary on individual paths. Below, √2⁢𝐷⁢𝑡 and 𝑣⁢𝑡 are equal at 4 s, when each is 0.40 degrees. Their squares are the separate contributions to the biased model’s MSD. The coordinate is unbounded, and these chosen values are not estimates from animal recordings.

records.alt: The first plot shows two positive peaked rate curves separated by a constant twenty spikes per second. The second shows their shared derivative, positive to the left, zero at the central peak and negative to the right. The third shows squared slope divided by rate for each curve. Both contributions vanish at the center and rise on the flanks; the higher baseline curve contributes less at every point with nonzero slope.
records.caption: Figure 3.1: Analytic teaching curves 𝑟𝐴⁡(𝜃) =5 +35⁢𝑒−𝜃2/(2⁢𝑤2) and 𝑟𝐵⁡(𝜃) =𝑟𝐴⁡(𝜃) +20, in spikes per second, with chosen width 𝑤 =0.6 rad. The rates have the same derivative. Their individual Poisson information contributions (𝑟′𝑖)2/𝑟𝑖 vanish at the rate peak, where the slope is zero, and are positive on the flanks. Adding baseline firing raises the count noise without changing the slope, reducing local information. These are illustrative tuning curves, not recorded neurons or a demonstrated attractor network.

records.alt: Across memory coordinates from minus one hundred sixty to one hundred sixty activation units, internal information has a minimum of 0.05 at zero and grows toward either side. Actual diffusion is a horizontal line at one thousand. The information lower bound meets it at zero and bends downward, reaching seven hundred fifty at coordinate one hundred. A marked gap separates actual diffusion from the bound there.
records.caption: Figure 3.2: Analytic teaching calculation for the chapter’s mutual inhibition example, with 𝑏 =200 activation units and 𝜏 =0.1 s. The coordinate 𝜃 is an activation difference. For positive rates 𝑟1,2 =(𝑏 ±𝜃)/(2⁢𝜏), 𝐽 =2000/(40000 −𝜃2) while 𝐷 =1000 activation units squared per second. The lower bound 1/(2⁢𝜏2⁢𝐽) equals 𝐷 at 𝜃 =0 and falls to 750 at 𝜃 =100. Higher local information permits a lower diffusion bound but leaves the actual diffusion unchanged in this model. The plotted range stays inside the positive-rate domain |𝜃| <200.

records.alt: Horizontal stacked bars use one variance axis in degrees squared: movement has common variance 0.00820 and other variance 0.00180; the single cell prediction has the same common variance and private variance 0.22446. A curve shows R falling as private predictor variance increases, reaching 0.170 at the constructed point, while χ remains 0.820.
records.caption: Figure 4.2: The same common variance enters movement and the single cell predictor, but the predictor has much more private noise. Increasing only private predictor variance lowers correlation R while the common movement fraction χ stays at 0.82. The marked point uses the chapter’s constructed example. Calculations assume unit common gain and mutually uncorrelated contributions; they are not recorded cell data. Based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 11–15.

records.alt: Movement MSD rises linearly from zero. For all strictly positive lags, observed MSD is higher by 0.0010 degrees squared. The observed curve has an open endpoint at lag zero, above the actual zero-lag point at zero. At 20 milliseconds the observed and corrected values are 0.0014 and 0.0004 degrees squared, with a bracket showing the subtraction and an uncertainty bar on the corrected value.
records.caption: Figure 4.3: For positive lags, independent measurement error adds 2⁢𝜎2𝑚 to the movement MSD, here 𝑀⁡(ℓ) =2⁢𝐷⁢ℓ. The isolated point at zero lag stays zero because each sample is subtracted from itself. At 20 ms, subtracting 0.0010 from 0.0014 deg² leaves 0.0004 deg²; the shown ±0.0001 deg² subtraction uncertainty is 25% of that remainder. Original analytic example, not experimental data, using Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 18–19.

records.alt: The upper plot shows one fixed smooth input against spatial position, with a threshold at 0.8 and shaded intervals above it. The lower plot uses the same positions and plots six times the positive excess above the threshold in hertz. Its connected positive intervals align with the upper shading; all other positions have zero firing.
records.caption: Figure 5.1: One fixed Gaussian input draw becomes a nonnegative firing map through 𝐹⁡(𝑥) =𝑎⁢[𝑧⁡(𝑥)−𝑞]+. Values below 𝑞 become zero; values above 𝑞 keep their relative heights after subtraction and scaling. The shaded connected intervals are the model fields. This is a simulated teaching map with chosen parameters, not a recorded cell. Based on Mainali et al. (2025), Fig. 1A and STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1.

records.alt: Three density curves against dimensionless size w show the one dimensional curve starting at zero, the two dimensional curve starting at one, and the three dimensional curve rising without bound toward zero size. An arrow marks the unbounded end. In the second panel, three differently styled survival curves coincide on exp(-u) after U=w^(2/d).
records.caption: Figure 5.4: The limiting size densities differ with spatial dimension: one dimensional length is Rayleigh, two dimensional area is exponential, and three dimensional volume has a density that rises without bound as size approaches zero, while its integral remains one. Their survival probabilities, the probabilities of exceeding a threshold, coincide after transformation to 𝑈 =𝛽⁢𝑠2/𝑑, where Pr⁡(𝑈 >𝑢) =𝑒−𝑢. These are exact calculations from the high-threshold limiting law, not finite-threshold simulations or measured histograms. Based on Mainali et al. (2025), main Eq. 1, p. 1111, and Methods S3.

records.alt: The upper plot shows two fixed linear tuning curves with slopes plus two and minus one hertz per meter, crossing at ten hertz. Moving from zero to plus 0.1 meter raises the first rate by 0.2 hertz and lowers the second by 0.1 hertz. The lower plot puts the paired rate changes on a downward sloping line through zero, with that example marked.
records.caption: Figure 6.1: A common displacement of +0.1 m increases rate 1 by 0.2 Hz and decreases rate 2 by 0.1 Hz. The changes lie on one line. With displacement variance 0.01 m², their covariance is −0.02 Hz² and their correlation is −1. The 10 Hz baseline is chosen only to display positive rates. These are exact lines from the guide’s local example, not recorded data.
